extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and advanced students concerned with scientific method and hypothesis testing
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming, testing, and accepting scientific hypotheses and explanations; covers when a law may be regarded as explained, the distinction between derivative and ultimate laws, and the proper use and limits of hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premises must be experimentally established
rubrics_metrics.description: The deductions which Bacon abolished were from premises hastily snatched up, or arbitrarily assumed. The principles were neither established by legitimate canons of experimental inquiry, nor the results tested by that indispensable element of a rational Deductive Method, verification by specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using deduction, ensure the premises are grounded in sound experimental evidence before deriving wide conclusions. Anti-pattern: building a deductive theory on untested or arbitrarily assumed axioms. Example: Newton’s use of an inverse-square law as an hypothesis that was then verified by deducing Kepler’s laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must be testable by legitimate induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To entitle an hypothesis to be received as one of the truths of nature ... it must be capable of being tested by the canons of legitimate induction, and must actually have been submitted to that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis is only provisionally useful until it has been subjected to inductive tests (observation/experiment). Evaluate hypotheses by whether they yield empirically testable consequences and whether those consequences have been tested. Scoring note: deductive success (deriving known facts) is promising but not sufficient without induction-based confirmation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as resolution into causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Explaining, in the scientific sense, means resolving a uniformity which is not a law of causation, into the laws of causation from which it results, or a complex law of causation into simpler and more general ones from which it is capable of being deductively inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess an explanation by its ability to reduce observed regularities to causal mechanisms or simpler general laws. Good explanations account for empirical regularities by showing how they follow from more basic causal relations. Anti-pattern: treating description or naming of regularity as explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish derivative from ultimate laws (recognize limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between two kinds of laws, or observed uniformities in nature: ultimate laws, and what may be termed derivative laws. Derivative laws are such as are deducible from, and may ... be resolved into, other and more general ones. Ultimate laws are those which can not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of reduction, determine whether the target law is genuinely derivative (resolvable into more general laws) or whether it points to an ultimate law (an irreducible element, e.g., a distinct sensation). Avoid expecting all phenomena to be resolvable into a single law; check whether further reduction would still leave an irreducible 'law of color' or similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for instances where law's conditions obtain
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature previously unknown has been brought to light ... [it is important] of examining all cases which present the conditions necessary for bringing that law into action; a process fertile in demonstrations of special laws previously unsuspected, and explanations of others already empirically known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test explanatory hypotheses by actively seeking and examining cases where the purported antecedent conditions are present. Use these instances to confirm, refine, or falsify the law. Practical method: apply the law to diverse contexts (e.g., Faraday’s magnet + conductor examples) to check scope and predictive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility by analogy to known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses of this sort would not have any of the plausibility belonging to those which ally themselves by analogy with known laws of nature ... Either the phenomenon assigned as the cause is real, but the law according to which it acts merely supposed; or the cause is fictitious, but is supposed to produce its effects according to laws similar to those of some known class of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer hypotheses that extend or analogize from established laws rather than inventing wholly novel agents and novel laws simultaneously. A plausible hypothesis often maps onto familiar mechanisms, aiding intelligibility and test design. Anti-pattern: inventing both an unobserved agent and a wholly unanalogous law without independent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses as provisional tools requiring eventual verification
rubrics_metrics.description: These general truths will doubtless make their first appearance in the character of hypotheses; not proved, nor even admitting of proof, in the first instance, but assumed as premises for the purpose of deducing from them the known laws of concrete phenomena. But this, though their initial, can not be their final state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheses as useful provisional constructs to generate deductions and guide experiment, but insist they progress from hypothesis to tested theory. Do not accept hypotheses permanently as final explanations without passing inductive tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary assumption of unproved entities or laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The really weak point in the attempts ... is not that the attempt itself is unphilosophical, but that the existence of the fluid, and the fact of its vibratory motion, are not proved, but are assumed, on no other ground than the facility they are supposed to afford of explaining the phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed explanatory entities by whether there is independent evidence for their existence. Do not grant explanatory status to entities introduced solely for explanatory convenience unless they can be independently detected or their consequences verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of attempting reduction, but with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea receives so much apparent countenance from the nature of the most remarkable achievements of modern science, that speculators are even now frequently appearing, who profess either to have solved the problem, or to suggest modes in which it may one day be solved. ... the attempt so to resolve them is perfectly legitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is philosophically acceptable to attempt to reduce classes of phenomena to more general laws (e.g., motion, heat, electricity), but such attempts must be guided by evidence and subject to empirical tests. Do not reject reductionist projects out of principle, nor accept them without rigorous testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate theories by their capacity to explain and improve empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical generalizations on which the operations of the arts have usually been founded, are continually justified and confirmed on the one hand, or corrected and improved on the other, by the discovery of the simpler scientific laws on which the efficacy of those operations depends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a theoretical account, consider whether it explains existing empiricisms and suggests better processes or corrections in applied practice (e.g., agriculture, medicine). The practical success of a theory in improving methods and clarifying intermediate links is a criterion of merit.
